title: The Art of League Tabling All Students, to Dramatically Improve Progress
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that ranking students can be fair, motivating and supportive if schools rank the right things. He recommends ranking effort and volume of work, retrieval-quiz performance, personal bests, and improvement from a pretest baseline rather than raw ability. He describes using homework scaffolds with model answers so every student can reach a high mark in class, and gradually reducing the scaffold until answers are produced cold. His most practical technique is narrating the room, calling out the number of lines each student has written at intervals so social norms pull effort up. He supports the case with an English department example in which ranking pages written raised average output from two to three pages, and with the point that students rank themselves anyway if teachers do not. The piece ends with promotion for his own books, but the classroom method is clearly argued.
points: Rank what is fair to rank, such as effort, volume, attempts and improvement, rather than innate ability.
Ranking improvement from a pretest baseline lets a grade 5 student top the table ahead of a grade 9 student, making the table motivating for all.
Narrating the room with line counts exploits students' wish to fit social norms and reduces the group that applies minimal effort.
Students respond to what is measured: league tabling pages written raised an English team's average from two to three pages.
quotes: Your number one principle has to be to rank in ways which are considered fair. Effort is always a fair measure. Measure the number of pages written, number of lines written, or time spent concentrating on the task.

With knowledge retrieval testing , it is completely fair to rank the numbers of questions attempted, and the percentage correct. Why? Because knowledge retrieval is simply testing what has already been taught. It is testing whether students have been paying attention to their learning. It isn’t another form of IQ test.
If we don’t rank students in this way, they do it themselves. They view themselves as failures if they are not in the top 30%.

A student gaining a grade 5 might well top the league table ahead of a student gaining a grade 9. It is human nature to want to improve, and if we can simply measure improvement, we will dramatically increase performance. And it is totally fair!

My favourite method is to walk the room two minutes into a written task. Pick a student at the end of a row who seems to have written a sufficient amount in the time and simply state how many lines they have written.
As soon as the team started to league table how many pages students wrote, the average increased to 3 pages. That’s a 50% improvement in effort for one slight shift of focus.
You aren’t doing these exam practices to give a kid a grade. You were doing them to build expertise, mastery, and subject knowledge.
